questions.prompt: What does an INNER JOIN return?
options: Only rows with a match in both tables
All rows from the left table
questions.explanation: INNER JOIN keeps matching pairs only. LEFT JOIN keeps all left rows; FULL OUTER keeps all rows from both.

questions.prompt: Which aggregate counts only non-NULL values in a column?
questions.explanation: COUNT(column) skips NULLs; COUNT(*) counts rows.

questions.prompt: Every column in the SELECT list of a grouped query must either be in GROUP BY or inside an aggregate function (in standard SQL).
questions.explanation: Otherwise the database cannot know which row's value to show. SQLite and MySQL (in some modes) are lenient, which can hide bugs.

questions.prompt: With 4 customers and orders 101-105 (customers 1 and 2 have two orders each, customer 3 has one, Dana has none), how many rows does this return?
questions.code:
SELECT c.name, o.id
FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id;
questions.explanation: LEFT JOIN returns one row per matching order (5) plus one row for Dana with NULL order columns: 6.

questions.prompt: This should list all customers with their count of paid orders (0 for none), but customers without paid orders disappear. Why?
questions.code:
SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS paid
FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.status = 'paid'
GROUP BY c.name;
options: The WHERE filter on o.status removes the NULL rows from the LEFT JOIN; move the condition into the ON clause
GROUP BY is missing a column
questions.explanation: WHERE runs after the join; rows with NULL status fail it, turning the LEFT JOIN into an inner join. `ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'paid'` keeps them.

questions.prompt: Which statements about HAVING are true? Select all that apply.
options: It can use aggregates such as SUM(amount) > 200
It replaces WHERE for filtering individual rows efficiently
questions.explanation: HAVING filters groups using aggregates. Row filters belong in WHERE, which runs earlier and reduces work.

questions.prompt: A report joins orders to order_items and sums orders.amount per customer. Totals are inflated for customers with multi-item orders. Why?
options: The join repeats each order row once per item, so SUM counts the order amount several times; aggregate items separately or sum at the right grain
The report needs DISTINCT on customers
questions.explanation: Joining to a child table changes the grain (one row per item). Summing a parent-level value at child grain double counts. This 'fan-out' is a classic reporting defect.

questions.prompt: You need each customer's most recent order. Which approach is reliable?
options: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC) and keep row 1
GROUP BY customer_id with MAX(created_at) and SELECT the other order columns too
questions.explanation: The window function picks a whole row per customer deterministically (id breaks ties). Selecting non-aggregated columns next to MAX is invalid in standard SQL and unreliable where allowed. LIMIT 1 gives one row overall.

coding.title: Paid revenue per customer
coding.prompt:
For every customer (including those with no orders), return `name` and `paid_total` = sum of **paid** order amounts (0 if none), ordered by `paid_total` descending, then name.

Expected: Ben 300.0, Asha 120.0, Chen 45.5, Dana 0.
coding.starter:
-- Write your query here
SELECT 1 AS placeholder;
coding.solution: SELECT c.name, COALESCE(SUM(o.amount), 0) AS paid_total FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'paid' GROUP BY c.id, c.name ORDER BY paid_total DESC, c.name;
coding.explanation: Putting the status filter in the ON clause keeps customers without paid orders; COALESCE turns their NULL sum into 0.
hints: LEFT JOIN with the status condition inside ON.

coding.title: Latest order per customer
coding.prompt:
Using a window function, return each customer's most recent order: `customer_id`, `order_id`, `created_at`, ordered by `customer_id`.

Expected: `1 | 102 | 2026-05-03`, `2 | 105 | 2026-05-07`, `3 | 104 | 2026-05-06`.
coding.starter:
-- Write your query here
SELECT 1 AS placeholder;
coding.solution: SELECT customer_id, order_id, created_at FROM (SELECT customer_id, id AS order_id, created_at, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC) AS rn FROM orders) WHERE rn = 1 ORDER BY customer_id;
coding.explanation: ROW_NUMBER numbers each customer's orders newest first; keeping rn = 1 returns exactly one full row per customer. ISO date strings sort correctly as text.
hints: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at DESC)
Wrap it in a subquery and filter rn = 1.

coding.title: Customers above a threshold
coding.prompt:
List `customer_id` and `total` (sum of all order amounts regardless of status) for customers whose total is greater than 150, ordered by `customer_id`.

Expected: `1 | 200.0`, `2 | 360.0`.
coding.starter:
-- Write your query here
SELECT 1 AS placeholder;
coding.solution: SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id HAVING SUM(amount) > 150 ORDER BY customer_id;
coding.explanation: Aggregates cannot be used in WHERE; HAVING filters groups after SUM is computed.
